We selected `r length(unique(detect_data_clean$NWFSCsampleID))` water samples collected at `r length(unique(detect_data_clean$station))` unique locations during the 2019 NOAA hake abundance survey (@fig-bubble), targeting surface, 50, 150, 300, and 500 m sampling depths at each station. We amplified and sequenced these samples in 1 technical replicate using MFU, 3 technical replicates using MV1, and 1 technical replicate using DL, resulting in 514 successfully amplified and sequenced samples (`r detect_data_clean %>% group_by(primer, NWFSCsampleID) %>% n_groups()` sample-primer combinations).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sp-detects
#| tbl-cap: "Scientific names, common names, taxonomic family, broad taxon category, preferred prey category, and detections for each cetacean species detected in our study area. Detections are split by primer, and MV1 detections are split by whether a species was detected in 1, 2, or 3 of the 3 total technical replicates for that primer."

table <- mmEcoEvo %>% 
  select(Species, common_name, Family, Broad_taxa, Prey.family) %>% 
  mutate(Prey.family = case_when(Prey.family == "invert"~"zooplankton/forage fish",
                                 Prey.family == "squid"~"cephalopods",
                                 Prey.family == "fish"~"bony fishes")) %>% 
  inner_join(detect_primer_techRep_species_clean, by = c("Species" = "BestTaxon")) %>% 
  rename("Common name" = common_name, "Prey family" = Prey.family, "Broad taxon" = Broad_taxa) %>% 
  #left_join(detect_per_primer_species_clean, by = c("Species" = "BestTaxon")) %>%
  mutate(`Broad taxon` = tolower(`Broad taxon`))

pander(table, split.tables = Inf)
```

Across all samples, we observed `r sum(detect_data_clean$Detected)` positive detections of `r length(unique(detect_data_clean$BestTaxon))` cetacean species, including 6 baleen whale species, 5 dolphin species, 2 porpoise species, and 3 beaked whale species (@tbl-sp-detects). Of these, `r nrow(detect_per_species_clean %>% filter(nDetect > 10))` species were observed more than 10 times, and `r nrow(detect_per_species_clean %>% filter(nDetect < 10))` were observed fewer than 10 times. We also detected bottlenose dolphins (*Tursiops truncatus*) one time, in a sample collected north of the known range of this species in the California Current [@carretta_etal24]. As noted in the methods section, we consider this detection likely to have resulted from lab contamination and removed it before downstream processing.

@fig-bubble illustrates the distribution of detections across sampling depths $z$, ignoring $xy$ distribution, for all cetacean species included in the study. Notably, our dataset includes one unexpected detection of a bowhead whale (*Balaena mysticetus*), not generally observed south of 63 N latitude in the Bering Sea since the end of commercial whaling and not known to ever inhabit the California Current [@rugh_etal03], as well as two detections of extremely rare saber-toothed whales (*Mesoplodon stejnegeri*), a cold-water beaked whale visually observed only twice in the Gulf of Alaska between 1986 and 2005 [@Hamilton2009a]. This species has not been visually observed in the California Current, but it has been detected acoustically [@simonis_etal20a] and stranded twice in May 2015, in Oregon and Washington [@Hamilton2009a; @moore_barlow17; @Becker2020].

Because both of these species are exceptionally rare, we manually verified these detections against all publicly available sequence data. For both species, we found that (1) the detected sequences were a 100% match to database sequences, (2) the next best match was to a species that is not found in the North Pacific Ocean (Southern right whale and Gray's beaked whale), and (3) the next best realistic matches differed by 5 bp to our bowhead whale sequence and 9 bp to our saber-toothed whale sequence. While 12S sequence data are not currently publicly available for some North Pacific beaked whale species (e.g. *M. carlhubbsi*, *M. perrini*, and *M. peruvianus*), we found that our target region differs by 5-16 bp among species within the Mesoplodont genus that do have sequence data. We therefore retain the species-level classification for our saber-toothed whale detections given its 100% match to a reference sequence for that species.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bubble
#| fig-cap: "Left: Distribution of detections across sampling depths for all species included in the study. Species are grouped into baleen whales (Balaenopteridae, Balaenidae, and Eschericthidae), dolphins/porpoises (Delphinidae and Phocoenidae), and beaked whales (Ziphiidae). Right: Geographic distribution of samples used in this study, acquired from water collected during a 2019 survey of hake distribution in the California Current."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

legend1 <- get_legend(detectDepth_bubble)
legend2 <- get_legend(map)

plots <- plot_grid(detectDepth_bubble + theme(legend.position = "none"),
                   map + theme(legend.position = "none"),
                   ncol = 2,
                   rel_widths = c(3, 1),
                   align = "v",
                   axis = "tblr")

legends <- plot_grid(legend1,
                     legend2,nrow = 1,
                     align = "v",
                     axis = "l",
                     rel_widths = c(1, 1))

plot_grid(plots,
  ggdraw() +
    draw_plot(legends, x = 0.15, y = 0,
      width = 0.7, height = 1),
  ncol = 1, rel_heights = c(1, 0.18))

```

#### Question 1: How does observation error affect POD of cetacean DNA?

Given the presence of cetacean eDNA in a sample, its POD is affected by primer choice (@fig-H2POD-obsbias, left). Assuming a single freeze/thaw cycle and technical replicate, MV1 had the highest expected POD ($\Omega_\text{m*t}$, `r round(mean(thaw1_pdetect %>% filter(Primer == "MV1") %>% pull("PDetect")), digits = 2)`), followed by DL (`r round(mean(thaw1_pdetect %>% filter(Primer == "DL1") %>% pull("PDetect")), digits = 2)`) and then MFU (`r round(mean(thaw1_pdetect %>% filter(Primer == "MFU") %>% pull("PDetect")), digits = 2)`). We note that DL was never run at one freeze/thaw cycle (only 2-6), so the reported POD at one cycle is an extrapolation. Using the mean posterior POD for each primer at one freeze/thaw cycle ($\Omega_{m*1}$), we calculated the expected rate of increase in POD with increasing technical replication by primer (@fig-H2POD-obsbias, middle). Based on our results, achieving a POD \>90% for cetacean DNA collected in a sample would require four technical replicates of MV1, \~5-6 technical replicates of DL, or seven technical replicates of MFU.

While increasing the number of technical replicates increases POD, the number of freeze/thaw cycles decreases POD (@fig-H2POD-obsbias, right), consistent with increased degradation with increasing freeze/thaw cycles. We found a relationship between freeze/thaw cycle and posterior estimates of POD for the longest primer in our study (DL, 360 bp), and a weaker relationship between freeze/thaw cycle and posterior POD for MV1 (202 bp). The effect of freeze/thaw cycles on MFU could not be estimated from these data: only 14 of 514 MFU replicates were run at more than one freeze/thaw cycle, nearly all on a single sequencing run, and the posterior slope (0.09, 95% CI −0.26 to 0.43) mainly reflects the prior.

Given our posterior estimates of POD by primer and number of freeze/thaw cycles, we calculated a sample-specific POD for each sample in our study, assuming cetacean DNA is present in the biological sample. Averaged across all samples in this study when accounting for freeze/thaw cycles, the mean POD for cetacean DNA in a single technical replicate of DL is 0.14, for MFU is 0.31, and for MV1 is 0.39. Despite the significant reduction in POD in our DL sequence with increasing degradation caused by increasing freeze/thaw cycles (lowest DL POD = 0.09), including an additional four replicates using primers that target shorter DNA fragments that were not as strongly affected by freeze/thaw cycle (MV1 and MFU) ensured a high overall POD for cetacean eDNA in a biological sample, conditional on its presence. We estimated the sample-specific predicted DNA POD for each sample in our study using the sample-specific parameters for number of freeze/thaw cycles and primer used in each technical replicate and calculating POD across all technical replicates for each sample combined. Using this approach, we determined that mean predicted POD across all samples in the study was `r round(mean(POD_per_samp$POD), digits = 2)` (range: `r round(min(POD_per_samp$POD), digits = 2)` - `r round(max(POD_per_samp$POD), digits = 2)`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-H2POD-obsbias
#| fig-cap: "Left: Posterior distribution of primer-specific POD (vertical axis) for cetacean eDNA given its presence in a sample (horizontal axis) assuming one freeze-thaw cycle. Middle: Posterior mean primer-specific POD (vertical axis) with increasing technical replication (horizontal axis) for each primer used in this study, also assuming one freeze/thaw cycle. Right: Posterior distribution of POD given presence (vertical axis) by number of freeze/thaw cycles (horizontal axis) and primer (panels). Dashed lines and lighter shading indicate extrapolation beyond the observed data."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

 pdetect_primer | Q2_TechRepsXPrimer | ppdetect

```

### Question 2: Does species-specific detection rate vary with depth?

In the next two sections we switch to considering detection rate of cetacean DNA in the ocean using five technical replicates per sample (3 MV1, 1 DL, 1 MFU), without assuming its presence in a biological sample. Detection rate varies with depth (p \<\< 0.001, deviance explained = 0.7%; Supplemental Figure S1); the model that best describes variance in detection rate with depth includes significant smooth terms for depth, species, and a depth x species interaction (AIC = `r round(min(modelAIC$AIC))`, @tbl-modelAIC). This model explained 13.2% of deviance in eDNA detection probability, with a mean AUC of `r round(mean(AUC_df_clean$AUC), digits = 2)` and a mean optimized TSS of `r round(max(TSS_df_clean$mean), digits = 2)`. Full model AUC and TSS values are shown in Supplemental Figure S2. Finally, we found general agreement between species-specific model predictions and raw detection data via visual comparison (Supplemental Figure S3).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-modelAIC
#| tbl-cap: "Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) values degrees of freedom ($df$) for all GAMs tested to characterize the relationship between depth and detection rate of eDNA. Models and stratification schemes from Eq. 4."

modelAICtable <- modelAIC %>% 
  arrange(AIC) %>% 
  mutate(minAIC = min(AIC)) %>% 
  mutate("$\u394 AIC$" = AIC-minAIC) %>% 
  mutate("Stratification" = case_when(model %in% c("m1.2", "m1.1")~"species",
                                      model == "m1.2a"~"family",
                                      model == "m1.2b"~"prey",
                                      model == "m1.0"~"none")) %>% 
  mutate(Model = case_when(model == "m1.2"~"$\u03b2_s + f_s(z)$",
                           model == "m1.1"~"$\u03b2_s + f(z)$",
                           model == "m1.2a"~"$\u03b2_F + f_F(z)$",
                           model == "m1.2b"~"$\u03b2_e + f_e(z)$",
                           model == "m1.0"~"$\u03b2_0 + f(z)$", 
                           TRUE~model)) %>% 
  mutate("$df$" = df) %>% 
  select(Model, Stratification, "$df$", "$\u394 AIC$")

kable(modelAICtable, escape = FALSE, digits = 1)
```

Broadly, delphinid detection rate was highest at the surface, beaked whale detection rate was highest at depths \> 200 m, and baleen whale detection rate was highest either at the surface or at depths \> 400 m (@fig-H1POD-species). Note that although detection data from the five species detected fewer than 10 times were included in our model input, we did not make predictions for any of these species.

Among the delphinids, species-specific trends in detection rate generally reflected previously developed estimates of time-at-depth [@watwood_buonantony12; @oliveira_etal]. Conversely, most beaked whale and baleen whale species in the study were very likely to be detected outside depths where they were estimated to spend most of their time (@fig-H1POD-species). Most notably, predicted detection rate depth distribuitons for two of the three baleen whales indicated a high detection rate at 500 m, while these two species spend most of their time above \~200 m depth. Per-species model predictions are shown alongside observed detections in Supplemental Figure S3.

```{r}
#| label: fig-H1POD-species
#| fig-cap: "Species-specific detection rate predictions across all depths sampled in this study. Solid line shows posterior predicted detection rates; shaded regions show 95%, 75%, and 50% confidence band. Dashed line shows relative time at depth, rescaled to the range of predicted detection rates for comparison of shape only. Plots are colored by broad taxonomic category as described in Table 1. The grey rug plot at the bottom shows sampled depths, and the colored rug plot at the top shows the depths of positive detections for each species."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

m1.2POD

```

Models stratifying detections by taxonomic family and preferred prey category both had higher AIC values than the model stratified by species (AIC = `r round(filter(modelAIC, model == "m1.2a")$AIC, digits = 0)` and `r round(filter(modelAIC, model == "m1.2b")$AIC, digits = 0)`, respectively), but still had significant terms for family and depth-by-family interactions (taxonomic model) and for prey type and depth-by-prey type interactions (prey type model). Predicted detection rate curves for each model illustrate varying trends in detection rate with depth across strata (@fig-H1POD-family-prey). Similar to the model stratified by species, we did not make predictions for families with fewer than 10 detections using the taxonomic model, which excluded the Balaenidae (bowhead whale family).

```{r}
#| label: fig-H1POD-family-prey
#| fig-cap: "Left: Detection rate by depth for species stratified by taxonomic family. Right: Detection rate by depth for species stratified based on broad prey categories. In both, the grey rug plot at the bottom shows sampled depths, and the colored rug plot at the top shows the depths of positive detections in each family or prey category."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

m1.2aPOD_bordered <- patchwork::wrap_elements(m1.2aPOD) +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 1))

m1.2bPOD_bordered <- patchwork::wrap_elements(m1.2bPOD) +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 1))

(m1.2aPOD_bordered + m1.2bPOD_bordered) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(3, 1), axis_titles = "collect") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

#### Question 3: Does depth variability in detection rate vary spatially?

For a subset of the data comprising the most frequently detected delphinid (Pacific white-sided dolphin, *Aethalodelphis obliquidens*), baleen whale (humpback whale, *Megaptera novaeangliae*), and beaked whale (northern giant bottlenose whale, *Berardius bairdii*), we found that covariability in $xyz$ (AIC = `r round(AIC(m3.0c), digits = 0)`, deviance explained = 26.3%) predicted species-specific detection rate better in our study area than variability in predicted density ($D$) and depth ($z$; AIC = `r round(AIC(m3.1), digits = 0)`, deviance explained = 10%). Significant terms in our $xyz$ model included an interaction between species and $xyz$, an interaction between species and $xy$, and an interaction between species and $z$. While the unfactored terms for $z$ and $xy$ were not significant, removing these terms increased model AIC to 1411. Mean AUC of our $xyz$ model across a 10-fold validation test was `r round(mean(AUC_df_m3.0c$AUC), digits = 2)` and mean optimized TSS was `r round(max(TSS_df_m3.0c$mean), digits = 2)`. Full model TSS for all thresholds are shown in Supplemental Table S3 and Supplemental Figure S2. Although adding $xy$ improved model performance, the predicted depth of maximum detection rate for the most frequently detected delphinid, baleen whale, and beaked whale exhibited only marginal variability across $x$ and $y$, largely adhering to the broad trends identified in Q2 (@fig-H3PODxy).

The Pacific white-side dolphin detection rate was maximized near the surface, with maximum detection rate at depths shallower than 100 m in 83% of the study area. The depth of maximum detection rate was deeper toward the south and east of the study area; however, model uncertainty increased in the same region. The predicted detection rate was less than 0.5% in two small regions near Cape Mendocino, representing approximately 3.5% of the study area.

The depth that maximized detection rate for northern giant bottlenose whales was greater than 150 m in 46% of the study area. An additional 33% of the study area had predicted detection rates less than 0.5% at all depths . Notably, the region where predicted detection rate was near zero was along the coastline and continental shelf region throughout the study area. Similar to patterns observed for the Pacific white-sided dolphin, the depth of maximum detection rate was deeper to the south and east of the study area, with increasing model uncertainty in the same region.

For humpback whales, there were two disparate peaks that maximized detection rate - shallower than 150 m or deeper than 450m - with no depths between 200 and 400 m maximizing detection rate throughout the study area. The predicted detection rate was maximized at depths shallower than 150 m in 46% of the study area, mainly along the coast and continental shelf, and was maximized at depths greater than 450 in 43% of the study area, mainly along the shelf break and in deeper water. Model uncertainty was greatest for this species along the shelf break representing the transition zone between the two depths, and small outside the transition zone. A small region offshore of Cape Mendocino had predicted detection rates lower than 0.5%, representing 1.5% of the study area.

Right: Model uncertainty represented as the strip width of depths within the 50% CI for maximum detection rate of the same three species. Observed detection depths are shown as colored points. While our model predicting detection rate across depth and predicted species' density did not perform as well as our $xyz$ model, the model included significant terms for the effect of predicted density on detection rate in two of the three species included in this section: Pacific white-sided dolphins and humpback whales. For both of these species, the predicted detection rate increased with predicted species' density (@fig-H3POD_D). There was no relationship between predicted species' density and predicted detection rate for northern giant bottlenose whales within the ranges of predicted species' densities that were included in our study area (0 - 0.017).
